Bénédictine and brandy have long been mixed, and the pairing first appears in cocktail books in the early 1900s as a layered pousse-café, with brandy floated over the liqueur, as in Raymond Sullivan's 1910 Barkeeper's Manual. Popular culture holds that the B & B was created in the 1930s, specifically in 1937 by a bartender at New York's 21 Club, though when and where it was first mixed is uncertain.

Its popularity is not in doubt. Around 1937 or 1938 Bénédictine began producing a bottled blend of 60% Bénédictine and 40% French brandy for the US market, and in America sales of the bottled B&B still exceed those of the original liqueur.
tasteProfile: Honeyed, spiced brandy in its simplest form. Cognac brings dried fruit, vanilla and gentle oak, while Bénédictine adds honey, warm baking spices and a subtle herbal complexity. Stirred and served over a large cube, it gradually softens as the ice melts. Smooth, rich and warming, slightly drier than the traditional equal-parts mix, it is a classic after-dinner digestif for a cold evening.
researchNotes: Origin disputed: layered Bénédictine and brandy in print by 1910 (Sullivan); popular claim of 1937 at New York's 21 Club is unverified. yearCreated 1910 = earliest print. Traditionally equal parts; Difford's uses slightly more brandy and notes some may add 10 ml water.
shortDescription: Cognac stirred with Bénédictine over ice: a honeyed, spiced after-dinner pairing so popular that it was later sold ready-bottled.

name: Rum Runner
garnish: Pineapple wedge and maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a hurricane glass and fill it with crushed ice.
Shake both rums, the banana liqueur, crème de mûre, pineapple juice, lime juice and grenadine with ice.
Strain into the glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.
history:
The Holiday Isle Tiki Bar in Islamorada in the Florida Keys claims to be the home of the Rum Runner. The bar opened in 1969 as The Hapi Hula Hut and was renamed in 1971. According to the bar's own account, which it presents as legend, manager John 'Tiki John' Elber needed to use up surplus rum and liqueurs before new stock arrived, so he mixed banana liqueur, Myers's rum, brandy and grenadine.

He named the result after the rum runners, the liquor smugglers who used the Florida Keys as their base during the early twentieth century. Difford's Guide's version moves away from that improvised mix, pairing Jamaican and Cuban rums with banana and blackberry liqueurs, pineapple, lime and grenadine.
tasteProfile: Fruity, rounded and tropical with a touch of rum funk. Jamaican rum adds rich molasses and ripe fruit, while light Cuban rum keeps the base clean. Banana liqueur gives a lush, sweet banana note and crème de mûre brings dark blackberry depth. Pineapple and lime make it juicy and tart, and grenadine adds colour and sweetness. Served over crushed ice, it is a cheerful beach-bar drink for hot days.
researchNotes: Origin is the Holiday Isle bar's own 'legend' (as quoted by Difford's); no firm creation date, so yearCreated null; era modern (bar opened 1969). The bar's original mix (banana liqueur, Myers's rum, brandy, grenadine) differs from Difford's spec. Difford's text has the typo 'Run Runner'.
shortDescription: Two rums shaken with banana and blackberry liqueurs, pineapple, lime and grenadine: a fruity Florida Keys tiki-bar classic.

name: Pink Squirrel
garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and a line of Creole-style (Peychaud's) bitters across the surface
instructions: Chill a Nick & Nora or coupe glass.
Shake the crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Dust with grated nutmeg and finish with a line of Creole-style bitters.
history:
The Pink Squirrel was created in 1941 by Bryant Sharp at Bryant's Cocktail Lounge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The original reportedly used ice cream rather than cream, and Difford's Guide suggests it may have begun life before Repeal as a spirit-spiked milkshake. Difford's credits Michael Lazar, known as Mr. Manhattan, for researching the drink's origins.

In the 1960s Bryant's second owner, Pat Malmberg, judged the crème de cacao unnecessary and removed it, and Bryant's still makes its Pink Squirrels that way. Difford's keeps the cacao, noting that some prefer heavy cream or equal parts of each ingredient.
tasteProfile: Light pink, sweet and creamy. Crème de noyaux brings a toasted almond, marzipan-like flavour and its signature rosy colour, while white crème de cacao adds soft milk-chocolate notes. Whipping cream gives a smooth, silky body, and the nutmeg and line of Creole bitters add warm spice and a faint anise lift. Indulgent and dessert-like, it is best enjoyed after dinner or as a festive treat.
researchNotes: No dictionary ID for crème de noyaux (almond/apricot-kernel liqueur, red); mapped to amaretto with note. Consider proposing 'creme-de-noyaux' if more recipes need it. Original reportedly used ice cream; Bryant's current house version omits crème de cacao. Nick & Nora mapped to Coupe.
shortDescription: Crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream shaken together: a pink, almond-and-chocolate dessert drink from 1941 Milwaukee.

name: Coffee Cocktail
garnish: Grated nutmeg
instructions: Shake the port, cognac, syrup and egg very thoroughly with ice.
Strain back into the shaker and dry shake without ice.
Strain into a small goblet or wine glass.
Grate a little nutmeg on top.
history:
The Coffee Cocktail is adapted from a recipe in the 1887 edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-Tenders Guide, published after the Professor's death in December 1885. It called for powdered sugar, a fresh egg, a large glass of port and a pony of brandy, shaken thoroughly with ice, strained into a bar goblet and finished with grated nutmeg.

The book itself admits the name is a misnomer, as the drink contains neither coffee nor bitters. It was probably so called because, properly mixed, it looks like a cup of coffee, with a creamy brown colour and a frothy head.
tasteProfile: Rich, velvety and gently sweet, like a fortified wine flip. Tawny port brings nutty, raisined and caramel notes, cognac adds warmth and dried-fruit depth, and the whole egg gives a thick, custard-like texture with a creamy foam. A little sugar rounds it out and grated nutmeg adds warm spice. Low in harshness and big on comfort, it is an ideal after-dinner or winter-evening drink.
researchNotes: Difford's page did not render its own method/glass section in the fetched HTML; method, goblet (mapped to Wine Glass) and nutmeg garnish follow the Jerry Thomas 1887 recipe quoted on the same page, with the dry shake as is usual for whole-egg drinks. Ingredient amounts are Difford's.
shortDescription: Tawny port and cognac shaken with a whole egg and sugar under nutmeg: an 1887 Jerry Thomas flip that only looks like coffee.

name: Royal Hawaiian
garnish: Skewered pineapple wedge (or dehydrated pineapple wheel) and maraschino cherry
instructions: Chill a coupe glass.
Shake the gin, pineapple juice, lemon juice and orgeat with ice.
Fine strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge or wheel and a cherry.
history:
The Royal Hawaiian was created in 1948 at the Moana Hotel on Waikiki Beach, Hawaii, and first appeared in print in Ted Saucier's 1951 Bottoms Up, credited to the hotel. That recipe shook gin with equal pineapple juice, a little lemon and a teaspoon of orgeat, served in a chilled champagne glass.

In 1953 the Moana's bungalows across the road were demolished to make way for the Princess Kaiulani Hotel, named after the last heir apparent to the Hawaiian throne, and the cocktail appears to have re-emerged there as the new hotel's signature drink.
tasteProfile: A fruity, almond-scented gin sour. London dry gin provides crisp juniper and botanicals, pineapple juice adds tropical sweetness and a soft, frothy texture when shaken, and lemon brings a bright, tart balance. Orgeat lends a gentle nutty, floral richness that recalls a Mai Tai. Served straight up, it is light and elegant, a lovely aperitif or summer drink for gin lovers who enjoy tiki flavours.
researchNotes: Saucier's 1951 recipe uses equal gin and pineapple and only a teaspoon of orgeat; Difford's increases the orgeat. The Princess Kaiulani re-emergence is presented by Difford's as 'it appears'.
shortDescription: Gin shaken with pineapple, lemon and orgeat: a fruity, almond-tinged 1948 Waikiki gin sour first printed in Ted Saucier's Bottoms Up.
